events.text:
🇵🇱🪖📉 Poland Sinks Deeper Into Debt to Fund Military Buildup
Poland is borrowing to equip its own army and has told NATO it will put no more money, for now, into buying US weapons for Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk gave NATO chief Mark Rutte two reasons for that decision this month. Poland already has a large budget deficit, and its own defense orders take priority.
One tank order shows how far those commitments run. Poland took delivery of the last of its first 180 South Korean K2 tanks in November 2025. By then it had already signed a second contract with Hyundai Rotem, worth about $6.5B, for another 180 tanks, support equipment and the technology to build some of them in Poland. Deliveries under that order are due to run through 2030.
To finance the deal, Poland’s state development bank signed loan agreements with Santander and South Korea’s export-import bank. That lets Poland place orders years ahead of delivery. It also means the country can take on debt before the equipment reaches its army.
The European Commission expects Poland’s economy to grow 3.5% this year, yet it forecasts a deficit of 7.1% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. Social benefits and interest payments are already weighing on the budget. By 2028, the Commission expects public debt to reach 73.5% of GDP, up from 59.6% in 2025.
Even the revenue increases in next year’s draft budget face a political hurdle. President Karol Nawrocki can veto legislation, and parliamentary elections are due in 2027. Moody’s cut Poland’s credit rating in September. On November 6, S&P cut its rating on Poland’s local-currency debt and kept its foreign-currency rating at A−, with a negative outlook.
Tusk’s government still plans to spend 4.51% of GDP on defense in 2027. The spending it has put on hold is Poland’s next contribution to a NATO program that pools allied money for US arms and ammunition for Kiev, including missiles for Patriot air defenses. Tusk says other Polish support for Ukraine will continue.
That leaves NATO’s other donors with a concrete choice. If they want to keep those US weapons packages funded at the same level, they will have to cover the share Poland is now unwilling to pay.

👁 Hackers breach US Air Force’s cloud network supporting aircraft and missiles
Hackers have infiltrated Cloud One, the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, Reuters reports, citing sources.
The breach was discovered during a system upgrade. Neither who was behind it nor whether any data was stolen is known.
The attackers exploited a software vulnerability to gain access to the platform's control layer, an insider is cited as saying. 
Such access could potentially expose information on aircraft readiness and spare-parts movements.
🟥 Cloud One brings together cloud services from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet to support dozens of military applications, including systems handling personnel records, logistics, aircraft maintenance and weapons inventories
🟥 it supports Cloud-Based Command and Control, which integrates air defense radar and other surveillance data from across North America
🟥 it also underpins the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 US Air Force sites worldwide
The breach adds to[ a growing string](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78296) of cyber incidents, including recent attacks involving the FBI, Pentagon, Treasury Department and intelligence agencies.

events.text:
🇮🇶 Iraq-Kurdistan standoff looms as Iran set to benefit from Baghdad’s centralization push
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s decision to bring all the border crossings in the northern Kurdish region and oilfields in several provinces under federal control has triggered a sharp response from Erbil.
 
The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has denounced the move as unconstitutional, accusing Baghdad of seeking to centralize power. Kurdish authorities have warned that any federal troops entering the region would face resistance from the Peshmerga forces. Al-Zaidi, however, has denied plans to deploy troops there.
🛢 Oil smuggling dilemma
Baghdad says the measures are aimed at curbing the illegal smuggling of Iraqi crude oil. It has also signaled plans to take control of oilfield operations in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala provinces. Al-Zaidi has demanded that the KRG refrain from issuing permits for the export of oil and petroleum products without authorization from[ Iraq’s Oil Ministry.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78268)
Kirkuk is home to some of Iraq’s largest oilfields, which have been under Kurdish control since 2014, when Peshmerga forces seized the area amid the fight against ISIS.
As part of the same push, the Federal Border Ports Authority has been ordered to take control of Iraqi Kurdistan’s border crossings with[ Turkey, Iran and Syria.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75813) Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has upheld Baghdad’s authority to take necessary security measures along all of the country’s borders with neighboring states.
🤔 Who benefits?
Reports suggest that al-Zaidi’s initiative for greater central control over the country’s oil and gas was encouraged [by the Trump administration](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72894). Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for the Middle East, has been a key advocate of the move, according to Middle East Eye.
Iran, however, could also stand to benefit, the outlet reports. Baghdad’s decision may have even been coordinated with Tehran, which has long pressed Iraqi Kurdistan to crack down on Kurdish militant groups [operating against Iran](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76809.).
Iran has viewed the region as a rare staging ground for extremist groups seeking to foment unrest in Iranian Kurdistan. Federal control and patrols along the Iranian border could make cross-border movements more transparent, allowing Baghdad to be held accountable for any paramilitary groups crossing the border.

📈 Oil prices climb as Middle East risks mount ahead of OPEC+ meeting
Brent and WTI are heading for their first weekly gains this month as renewed threats to Middle Eastern oil supplies fuel market uncertainty, the WSJ reports.
Brent rose 0.6% to $97.15 a barrel on Friday, while US WTI jumped 2.7% to $85.96.
The rally comes amid fresh attacks on energy infrastructure: a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery sparked a fire and temporarily halted some operations, while a drone attack in Kuwait killed two Italian technicians.
👉 Traders are also watching Sunday's OPEC+ meeting, where producers are expected to discuss output policy for 2027. Disruptions caused by the war against Iran have complicated efforts to assess production capacity and set quotas.
Whether the group restores supply, maintains current restrictions or considers further cuts remains unclear. But for now, geopolitical risks are overshadowing the upcoming OPEC+ decision.
